claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the starting state is a simple, homogeneous FCC solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The low hardness and strength of the starting alloy are governed by intrinsically high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy promotes dynamic recovery through dislocation cross-slip and annihilation during deformation.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation and the formation of strengthening barriers.
Limited dislocation accumulation reduces strain hardening, hardness, and strength.
Cryogenic deformation suppresses the thermally activated mobility required for dynamic recovery relative to room-temperature deformation.
Suppressing dynamic recovery permits greater dislocation storage.
Cryogenically deformed samples should have a higher dislocation density than room-temperature-deformed samples.
Cryogenically deformed samples should have greater hardness than room-temperature-deformed samples.
Cryogenically deformed samples should have greater yield strength than room-temperature-deformed samples.
The controlled comparison uses identically processed samples deformed to the same strain at the same strain rate, with temperature as the only varied parameter.
The proposed loading mode is uniaxial tension at room temperature versus cryogenic temperature.
The hypothesis is restricted to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple FCC solid-solution state.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in dislocation density, hardness, and yield strength under cryogenic deformation would falsify the proposed dynamic-recovery explanation.
